scenes.title: What is the Command Line?
scenes.narration: The command line is a text-based way to talk directly to your computer by typing instructions instead of clicking.

scenes.title: Why Data Engineers Live Here
bullets: Servers rarely have a graphical interface, so the command line is often your only way in.
Typed commands are repeatable and scriptable, which makes automating data pipelines far easier.
It is dramatically faster than clicking through menus once you know the commands.
scenes.narration: Most production servers ship without a desktop, so the terminal is frequently the only door you have into a machine. Because every command is just text, you can save it, replay it, and wrap it in scripts to automate repetitive data work. And once the muscle memory sets in, typing beats clicking for almost everything.

scenes.title: GUI vs. Command Line
scenes.narration: A graphical interface is welcoming and visual, but it hides what is really happening and resists automation. The command line asks you to learn a vocabulary, yet in return it gives you precision and the ability to script anything. As a rule, reach for the terminal whenever a task needs to be repeated or run on a remote server.

scenes.title: Your First Commands
scenes.code:
whoami        # who am I logged in as?
pwd           # print working directory
ls            # list files here
echo "hello"  # print text back to me
scenes.narration: Every command follows the same rhythm: a command name, then optional arguments. Here whoami tells you your username, pwd shows where you currently are in the file system, and ls lists what is around you. The echo command simply prints text back, which becomes surprisingly useful inside scripts.

scenes.text: The command line is just a conversation with your computer in text — learn a handful of commands and the rest of data engineering opens up.
scenes.narration: Think of the terminal as a plain-text conversation with your machine. Master a small core of commands and every later topic becomes far more approachable.
